data.title: Business-Critical Services Can Be Stopped by Compromised Accounts
data.summary:
Accounts without an operational need could stop services supporting business-critical
functions, and the resulting outage would not be distinguished from a fault.
data.description:
Availability attacks need no sophistication where permissions are broad. Stopping a
service is a supported administrative action that leaves little trace and is usually
attributed to a fault rather than to an intrusion.

That attribution is the problem. An outage investigated as a technical failure consumes
the response window, and the organisation may restore service repeatedly without ever
considering that something is causing it.

The underlying issue is permission scope: service control rights granted broadly because
it was convenient, rather than to the accounts that operate the service.
data.recommendation:
* Restrict service control permissions to the accounts that operate each service.
* Alert on unexpected service stops for business-critical services and route the alert to
  security as well as to operations.
* Include deliberate disruption in incident response scenarios so an outage is not assumed
  to be a fault.
data.short_recommendation: Scope service control rights and route unexpected stops to security.
